cues.text: What needs to stay the same? One key thing that the European Union must keep is its ability to set high goals and targets
Goals are essential for success without clear goals. It becomes much harder to achieve meaningful change or improvement
They give people communities and countries something to work towards
The EU has many different goals, but some of the most important ones focus on sustainability and improving people's lives
A good example is the 17 Sustainable Development Goals, which were created by the United Nations.
These goals aim to improve conditions around the world in areas such as poverty, education, equality, clean water and the environment.
The EU supports these goals and is working towards achieving them by 2030.
Another important area is climate change. The EU should continue setting ambitious targets to reduce pollution, lower greenhouse gas emissions and protect the environment.
Climate change is a major challenge and taking action now will help protect future generations. The EU cannot afford to become satisfied with the progress it has already made.
Instead, it should continue searching for new ways to improve.
Overall, it is essential that the EU needs to maintain its ambition and its ability to
set high goals.
Whether the focus is sustainability, equality, education or environmental protection, clear
targets give countries something to work towards.
If the EU continues to aim high, it can improve the lives of its citizens while helping to
create a better world.

the case for dropping unanimity. So why not just get rid of it? Supporters of reform make a few
key arguments. Faster decision-making for one. The EU could act decisively on foreign policy
instead of waiting on whichever government decides to play hardball. Enlargement is another reason.
Unanimity exists for a reason.
It stops smaller countries from being steamrolled by heavyweights like France or Germany on
issues that matter to them most.
Foreign policy and tax are also deeply tied to national identity, which means many governments
would simply refuse to sign away their veto.
And here's the paradox.
Changing the rules requires unanimity too.
So the very system that needs reforming is what blocks its own reform.
There's also a real risk of a two-tier EU emerging where some countries push ahead with
deeper integration and others get left behind, deepening the divide rather than fixing it.
1. Possible middle ground solutions. Fortunately, abolishing unanimity isn't the only option
on the table. One existing tool is constructive abstention, where a country can simply step
aside from a vote instead of blocking it outright, letting the rest of the EU move forward.
Conclusion In our view, the EU should extend QMV to foreign
policy and sanctions specifically.
Taxation and treaty changes, though, are a different story.
our view of the EU in 2050.
Climate and environment. In 2050 the European Union will use energy that
comes from clean sources.
The European Union will rely on resources
in each country to create clean energy. For example the European Union will let
Ireland use its wind to generate energy and
will let Spain use solar panels to capture strong sunlight.
The EU will build connections between countries so that every country can access that energy.
It will need systems for transport and for removing carbon from the air.
The EU will make buses, trains and trams available in every city.
It will invest money to make these services more reliable and functional.
The European Union will see that better services will attract more people
and it will reduce the need for cars.
It will treat waste differently from today.
The EU will see that companies will change their way of working.
It will encourage companies to build things that last for years, not to break once a
guarantee ends.
European Union will also need people to change. It will ask whether people will choose quality
over convenience. The EU will see that this change is as important as the changes made
by companies or governments. If it succeeds, all parts will work together.
Tech and defence independence. By 2050, the European Union will stop relying on powers for technology.
It will change that. The European Union will invest in chip manufacturing, data centres and the European AI research.
The European Union will aim for no dependence on external sources for tools that the entire
continent needs.
It will avoid a crisis in another country from cutting access to services.
Digital sovereignty will go beyond a promise for the European Union.
Digital sovereignty will become part of hospital operation, bank operation and school teaching.
Everything will run on infrastructure that the European Union controls.
The EU will have one identity for every citizen that works across all member states.
The European Union will make accessing healthcare in Poland as simple as accessing it in Portugal.
The EU will remove forms and lost documents.
The European Union will use one identity and one system.
Security will look completely different for the European Union.
It will no longer depend on NATO or especially the United States for defence.
The EU will create an army.
The EU will not train together or share statements,
but will build a coordinated force with unified command.
The EU will let member countries keep their armies.
When the European Union faces a threat, the EU will make decisions quickly.
The European Union will not wait for 27 separate parliaments to agree.
It will find that the process is faster, stronger and more united.
This vision depends on something harder to create than machines or weapons for the European Union.
It depends on trust.
The EU will ask whether France, Germany, Poland and every smaller nation can truly agree to share power.
It will ask whether they can let go of some control to work together at a level.
The EU will see that this is the challenge.
It will recognize that technology and weapons are easier to build.
The European Union will realise that trusting each other enough to use them is not easy.
How the EU funds its member states The EU is funded through several streams,
one being contributions from member countries based on their wealth.
Contribution from member countries has been a controversial topic over the years.
There are many questions that have arisen over how much member states contribute to
the EU compared to how much funding they receive from the EU in forms such as grants.
The contributions are primarily calculated based off each member state's gross national
income, GNI, and applying a uniform rate meaning each country pays a different
amount, richer countries pay more and poorer countries pay less.
Where there is some controversy is how much countries take from the EU compared to how much they gave.

what Ireland should do to benefit more from the EU.
Ireland has gained benefits from being a member of the European Union.
These include access to the single market, EU funding,
education opportunities and closer cooperation with European countries.
Ireland could still do more to make the most of its EU membership.
One key area is EU funding. Ireland gets support from agriculture, infrastructure, education and regional development.
The government could do more to help businesses, community groups and local organisations understand how to apply for this funding.
With support, more of these groups could benefit and grow.
Ireland could also take advantage of European research and innovation programmes.
By working with universities and businesses across Europe,
Ireland could develop technologies, create high-skilled jobs
and improve areas like healthcare, artificial intelligence and renewable energy.
Collaborating with countries opens up more possibilities for innovation.
The single market is another opportunity.
Irish businesses can sell their products and services to customers in all EU countries
without facing many of the trade barriers that exist with non-EU countries.
The government could help smaller Irish companies understand the EU regulations and support
them into expanding into European markets.
Ireland should also focus on energy, especially offshore wind.
The country has strong wind resources and investing in this area could create jobs, reduce reliance on fossil fuels and help meet Europe's clean energy goals.
Offshore wind has potential and Ireland is well placed to benefit.
Education is another way Ireland can gain more from the EU.
Programs such as Erasmus allow students and young people to study, train and work in European countries.
Increasing participation in these programs could help Irish students gain real-world experience,
learn languages and build international connections.
Overall, Ireland could benefit more from the EU by making use of available funding, supporting
businesses and investing in research and renewable energy, and increasing educational opportunities.
By working with other EU countries, Ireland could make the most of opportunities that
the EU membership provides.
